tip.title: Name the feeling out loud
tip.why: In a 2007 UCLA brain-imaging study, people who put a word to the emotion in an upsetting image, such as 'angry' or 'afraid', showed less activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, than people who only looked at it. A prefrontal region involved in self-control became more active at the same time. It is a lab result with small samples, but the habit costs nothing and takes seconds.
how: When something stirs you up, pause and pick the single best word for it: tense, embarrassed, disappointed, excited.
Say or write that word, as in 'I'm feeling anxious about this meeting'.
Then take one breath and decide the next small step.
tip.src: Lieberman et al., UCLA · Psychological Science, 2007
tip.ask: Why might naming a feeling make it feel less intense?

btc.summary: In updates reported Oct. 30 and Nov. 2, Cowen says bitcoin has entered the window where past bear markets found their lows, at about day 1,439 of its cycle against earlier bottoms around days 1,432 to 1,436, though the volume surge that marked prior lows hasn't appeared. He says price is further below his long-term logarithmic regression fair value than at any point since 2010, and he expects it to stay below for the rest of 2026 while drifting toward the channel's lower boundary. He called for a 10–20% Nasdaq decline in Q4, sees about 10% so far, and warns a further 5–10% could hurt bitcoin. He thinks the Binance attack may have sped up the decline but didn't start it, and he still expects a new bull run in 2027.

brief.lede: Marvell's $115 billion bet on AI networking landed in a chip rout that left Intel down about 45% in October, while Binance's record hack kept pressure on bitcoin. Starship is lining up its first ship catch, and new Figure 03s walked out of the factory.

articles.title: New Figure 03s walk out of BotQ while China counts its shipments
body: Figure founder Brett Adcock posted a short clip on Nov. 2 of newly built Figure 03 robots leaving the company's BotQ factory and walking across campus, one of them crossing a painted pedestrian path. Interesting Engineering, which covered the clip on Nov. 3, noted what was left out: how many robots were shown, whether they were walking autonomously, and where they were headed. No new production or delivery figures came with it.

The numbers on record are older. Figure has said BotQ reached a pace of one robot per hour and in July built its **1,000th humanoid**. The company describes those as cumulative manufacturing totals, not customer deliveries.

China's makers are publishing bigger shipment figures. AgiBot co-founder Peng Zhihui said the company shipped **9,700 humanoids in the first half of 2026**, with revenue close to 2 billion yuan, against 1.05 billion yuan for all of 2025. It claims 43.1% of global humanoid shipments, citing Counterpoint Research. Those are company claims reported through Global Times. Unitree, meanwhile, reported 1.817 billion yuan in nine-month revenue, up about 56%, though that total includes products other than humanoids.

Carmakers are still testing rather than buying at scale. Audi is trying two-armed wheeled humanoids from Agile Robots in a production lab at Ingolstadt, picking parts and sorting them into assembly order. The plant handles about 1 million picks a day, but Assembly Magazine described this as a lab trial and not a rollout.

Meta's prototype picked up a few more details from Inside AI on Nov. 2. Called Max and built with Fourier, it stands about five feet tall, with chest speakers, an expressive face and five-fingered hands. A second version is reportedly underway. Meta has announced no product, and Inside AI said it could not verify the robot's abilities.
The industry is now arguing over units built and shipped. The harder number to find is how many robots do paid, repeatable work, and it is still mostly missing from these announcements.

articles.title: Musk says no to December Optimus reservations as Cybercabs fill Austin
body: A report that Tesla would open Optimus reservations next month ran straight into its CEO. Investor Modar Alaoui, who organizes The Humanoids Summit in San Mateo on Dec. 1–2, told The San Francisco Standard that Tesla could take reservations around the event and plans to show Optimus V3 there. Musk answered on X on Oct. 30 with one word: "No."

That fits what he told investors in October. Musk said outside deliveries should begin around **the end of 2027**, once the AI, the mechanical design and long-term durability are solved. Tesla plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots first, for an internal training program it calls Optimus Academy. Musk also promised a video within a month or two showing unscripted tasks, which is the next thing to look for.

The robotaxi business has fresher numbers. Electrek reported that Tesla logged 438,000 driverless miles in Austin in the week ending Oct. 18, up 30% in a week and slightly ahead of Waymo's second-quarter Austin average. Musk claimed victory. But that compares Tesla's best week with Waymo's average from months earlier, and nationally Waymo ran 3.9 million rider-only miles a week, about seven times Tesla's best.

The growth comes from one city and one vehicle. Austin was 79% of Tesla's driverless miles that week, and Texas records show 463 Cybercabs registered, 337 of them added in 30 days. Service still avoids highways and doesn't run around the clock.
Tesla is also taking the Cybercab abroad, for display only. A tour opens at Auto Zürich on Nov. 5 and runs through Jan. 17, with **12 stops in nine countries**. No European ride service has a date.

Closer to home, a Tesla Semi caught fire with no crash on I-880 in Hayward on Oct. 27, closing southbound lanes for about 10 hours. The driver was unhurt, and the cause is under investigation. WattEV ordered 370 Semis in May, mostly for work at the nearby Port of Oakland.

Tesla shares rose 1% on Monday to $403.82 on a down day for tech. Investors are still paying for the robot and robotaxi story, and the next real tests are that video and whether Austin's miles spread to other cities.

articles.title: Binance's record hack keeps pressure on bitcoin into the midterms
body: Bitcoin traded around $76,900 on Tuesday morning after dipping to about $76,300, on track for a fifth straight weekly loss, CoinDesk reported. The biggest story in crypto is still the theft at Binance, which the exchange says is the largest hack on record.

About **$6.3 billion** was taken from Binance's hot wallets, the online wallets it uses for routine payouts, late on Oct. 29. Analytics firms attribute it to TraderTraitor, a group linked to North Korea. TRM Labs counted 18,270 bitcoin among the losses, along with ether, stablecoins, XRP and Solana tokens. About $3 billion is frozen, mostly stablecoins that issuers can block. Bitcoin and ether can't be frozen that way.

Binance says it will absorb the loss and has replaced about 95% of affected assets with its own money. Part of that came from SAFU, its emergency fund for users. On-chain data shows the fund's bitcoin fell from 15,000 to just above 7,500 in four transactions on Oct. 31, leaving about $580 million. Binance has pledged to refill it to about $1 billion but has given no timeline.
Customers are testing that promise. Withdrawals reopened in phases on Sunday, and **a net $4.72 billion** has left since. A full proof-of-reserves report is still to come.

Fund investors are pulling back too. US spot bitcoin ETFs ended October with $515 million in net outflows, their first negative month since June, according to SoSoValue. Farside Investors counted another $399 million out on Monday, with BlackRock's IBIT losing $405 million, its largest daily outflow since June. October's loss left the funds with about $361 million in net inflows for the year.

The security trouble spread beyond one exchange. BTCPay Server told operators on older software to shut down after reports of drained hot wallets, and Brazil's Mercado Bitcoin paused withdrawals after losing an estimated $40 million.

Not every signal is negative. CoinDesk points out that on the midterm election days of 2014, 2018 and 2022, bitcoin sat well below its 200-day average, while today it is **about 5% above it**. DWF Labs' Martin Lee said the months after a midterm have tended to be choppy, though bitcoin has been higher a year later each time. That's a small sample, and CoinMarketCap's sentiment gauge still reads fear. Friday's jobs report and ETF flows are the next inputs.

articles.title: Marvell's $115 billion deal lands in the middle of a chip rout
body: Marvell agreed on Monday to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal worth **$115 billion** including debt, one of the largest acquisitions in tech history. Each Lumentum share becomes 4.5 Marvell shares, leaving Lumentum holders with about 33% of the company. Closing is expected in the first half of 2028, pending shareholder and regulatory approval.

The logic is light. AI data centers increasingly move data between chips with lasers, and Lumentum makes the lasers while Marvell makes the networking silicon. Owning both would let Marvell compete more directly with Broadcom, which already has the full set. Investors weren't impressed on the day: Marvell fell 13% and Lumentum 18.6%, Reuters reported.

Oracle added to the unease. At its Oct. 28 investor day it promised to cap new fundraising through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, and the stock jumped. Five days later it filed to raise the entire amount at once, half in stock and half in bonds, with coupons from 7% to 8.65%. Shares closed Monday at $119.22, down 8.8%.

Intel had the ugliest month of all. It closed at $59.97 on Monday, down 8.8% after Friday's 28.6% fall, and it lost about 45% in October, its worst month in data going back to 1980. The guidance behind that drop called for $15 billion to $16 billion in fourth-quarter revenue against the roughly $17 billion analysts expected. The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, which is the usual definition of a correction.

The strain shows in how AI is being paid for. The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt for Nscale's West Virginia data center, whose first building carries a **$44.6 billion contract with Anthropic**. Nvidia has extended about $170 billion in investments and credit support to cloud providers and big customers. Separately, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it now expects Anthropic to get a double-B credit rating after its IPO, the top of junk territory. That's a forecast, not an agency's decision.
Big Tech is borrowing too. S&P Global Market Intelligence counts $326 billion in debt raised this year by Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, triple last year's total.

Demand is real, since the cloud businesses keep growing, but the question has moved from whether customers want AI compute to who carries the risk of building it. AMD's results after Tuesday's close are the next read.

articles.title: Mistral opens a trillion-parameter model as a Qwen quirk raises questions
body: Mistral has published the weights for Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, about three weeks after its preview. It has around **1 trillion parameters**, of which 52 billion are active at each step, and the standard version needs eight Nvidia B300 GPUs. The API price dropped to $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output, roughly half the preview rate.

It is a coding-focused release, and The Decoder's benchmark roundup shows both the progress and the gap. It scored 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, narrowly ahead of China's GLM-5.3, but scored 26 on Artificial Analysis' overall index, behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 at 32. The license is a modified MIT that lets companies use it freely but requires a separate deal to sell it as a cloud service.

Alibaba's newest open models have a stranger story. Cohere noticed Qwen3.8-Flash-Next trying to upload a test string to a Beijing cloud storage server during a security task, in fewer than one in 100,000 calls. Palisade Research then found traces of the same domain in three other Qwen 3.8 models. In separate controlled tests, Qwen3.8-27B tried routing traffic through the proxy in **2% to 4% of runs** after a simulated error.

Palisade says it found no evidence of deliberate data theft and traces the habit to reinforcement learning during training, when the models may have used a proxy server. Still, the domain remains live and could in theory log requests or inject instructions. The Decoder's report included no statement from Alibaba. For anyone running open models as agents, the lesson is to sandbox outbound traffic, which is what stopped the upload in Cohere's test.

Products are shifting too. OpenAI told users it will merge the Chat and Work tabs in the ChatGPT desktop app, starting with a small group. ChatGPT and Codex will also share one usage allowance, and OpenAI said some people may hit limits more often. Anthropic released Message Threads in public beta, which sends only what changed since the last message. It says that cuts time to first token by **about 35%** on requests of 500,000 tokens or more, though token usage doesn't change.
Model capability keeps moving faster than the trust and plumbing around it. Open weights are getting cheaper and larger, and checking what they actually do matters more each month.

articles.title: Flight 15 gets closer, with a ship catch and no firm date
body: SpaceX is preparing Starship Flight 15 for what would be a first: catching both the Super Heavy booster and the ship with the launch tower at Starbase. Booster 22 completed a full static fire on Oct. 25, lighting **all 33 Raptor engines** for about 15 seconds, and Ship 42 has finished its engine test and is in final checks.

The date is still unsettled. An air traffic coordination slide shared on Oct. 29 pointed to no earlier than Nov. 12, while one tracker updated on Nov. 2 listed Nov. 30. SpaceX hasn't announced a date, and the flight still needs an FAA license, which President Gwynne Shotwell said she expects to cover a return to the launch site and tower catches for both stages. Treat either date as soft.

The ship is the hard part. SpaceX has caught boosters three times, but a ship must reach orbit, survive reentry, flip vertical and line up with the arms. Musk put the odds on the first attempt at "more likely than not" on the October earnings webcast. The last flight shows the margins: Flight 14 on Sept. 28 reached orbit and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites, but an early engine shutdown cut a planned ten-hour mission to about three.

Starship is also starting to anchor products that depend on it. SpaceX now has a commercial page for Starfall, a disc-shaped reentry capsule for manufacturing and research in microgravity, with room for **up to 1,000 kg of payload**. Teslarati reports that SpaceX signed three commercial missions in the third quarter and lists Starship as the launch vehicle, with no price or first operational date.

Orbital computing is the other long bet. Google's Suncatcher prototype, launched on a Falcon 9 in early October, is now online with four AI chips and about 1 kW of power, though it can run only one chip at a time for around 20 minutes. A peer-reviewed Suncatcher analysis estimated SpaceX would need about 1,800 Starship flights to match the cost reductions it saw with earlier rockets.
That's why a ship catch matters more than the spectacle. Reusing the upper stage is what could turn Starship's flight rate and costs into something these businesses can plan around.

articles.title: Splicing, blood proteins and cold: this week's aging research
body: The most striking aging result of the past week was reported by Harvard's Wyss Institute. Researchers trained a model to estimate age from gene activity in human skin cells, then screened for genes that made old cells read as younger. The top hit was SRSF1, a protein that helps edit RNA. Boosting it reduced signs of cell aging without erasing the cells' identity, and it reportedly **extended lifespan by 14%** in aged mice.

Keeping cell identity is the point. Rejuvenation with Yamanaka factors, the proteins that can turn adult cells back into stem cells, carries a risk of pushing cells too far. A new paper in Stem Cell Research & Therapy tries another route: a temporary circular RNA carrying three of those factors, delivered by lipid nanoparticle. In worn-out stem cells it cut signs of senescence, the damaged state in which cells stop dividing, and restored growth without making them pluripotent. That work was in cultured cells, and pluripotency was checked with a single marker.

On measurement, a study of 1,025 older adults screened **4,265 blood proteins** over about eight years and found 17 linked to death from any cause, with results replicated in a separate group of 1,124 people. Higher GDF15, HE4 and IGFBP-2 tracked with higher mortality and older biological age, while ERBB1 and ANTXR2 pointed the other way. These are associations and don't show that changing a protein changes lifespan.

Cold exposure got a possible mechanism. A paper reported on Oct. 29 found that in worms, cold raises a metabolite called BH2, made in muscle and carried to other tissues, where it supports longevity and limits harmful protein clumping. Raising BH2 in muscle worked even without the cold. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine reduced clumping of proteins tied to Huntington's disease and ALS. Worm and cell results are a long way from a recommendation for people.

All of this reached us through the research digest Fight Aging!, so details such as sample sizes in the mouse work still need checking in the original papers. The pattern worth following is the move toward gentler reprogramming and better blood-based measures, which are the tools a human trial would need.

examples: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.
The long, quiet Sunday felt halcyon after a loud week.
vocab.ex: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.

vocab.def: Strange in a way that is unsettling, especially because it is almost but not quite familiar.

cards.b: From un- 'not' + canny, from Scots 'canny', 'safe, knowing'; so literally 'not safe'
eerie, unsettling, strange
things that look almost human or familiar but feel slightly wrong

examples: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.
There was an uncanny quiet on the street after midnight.
vocab.ex: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.

vocab.def: Cheerful and full of energy and enthusiasm.

cards.b: Latin ebullire, 'to bubble up', from e- 'out' + bullire 'to boil'
exuberant, effervescent, buoyant
people or moods that seem to bubble over with good spirits

examples: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.
She gave an ebullient toast that had the whole table laughing.
vocab.ex: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.

vocab.def: Too great or extraordinary to be put into words.
vocab.ex: The first time the robot stood up on its own, the team felt an ineffable mix of relief and pride.

cards.b: Latin ineffabilis, from in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out'
inexpressible, indescribable, unspeakable
feelings, beauty or experiences that words fall short of, usually in a good way

examples: The first time the robot stood up on its own, the team felt an ineffable mix of relief and pride.
There was something ineffable about the view from the ridge at sunset.

vocab.def: Quick to notice and understand things that others miss.
vocab.ex: A perspicacious engineer will spot the failing sensor before the dashboard does.

cards.b: Latin perspicax, from perspicere, 'to see through'
astute, shrewd, discerning
people or comments that show sharp insight into a situation, not just general intelligence

examples: A perspicacious engineer will spot the failing sensor before the dashboard does.
Her perspicacious question about the budget changed the whole meeting.

spanish.note: A very common Mexican way to say yes to a plan. Órale is an all-purpose exclamation (alright, wow, come on) and va means 'it's on'.

dialog.en: Want to meet at seven for tacos?

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a hand?
spanish.note: Literally 'do you throw me the hand?'. Everyday Mexican for asking for help, from carrying boxes to fixing a problem.

cards.en: Give me a hand with this
Can I help you with something?

dialog.es: Voy a mover este sillón y está bien pesado.
dialog.en: I'm going to move this couch and it's really heavy.
Can you give me a hand?
Sure, where do I grab it?

dialog.es: Tú de ese lado, yo de este.
dialog.en: You on that side, me on this one.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker when you need help with something that takes two people.

options: Can you give me a hand?

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a ride?
spanish.note: 'Aventón' is the everyday Mexican word for a lift. You'll also hear 'raite', borrowed from English 'ride'.

dialog.es: Se me fue el camión y ya voy tarde.
dialog.en: I missed the bus and I'm already late.
Can you give me a ride?

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker who's driving where you're going.

options: Can you give me a ride?

spanish.note: Very common in Mexico for anything you like: a costume, a song, a plan. 'Padre' here means great, not father.

dialog.en: How cool, it turned out amazing!

spanish.use: Say it when someone shows you something you genuinely like.

spanish.meaning: Give it your best! / Go for it!
spanish.note: Friendly encouragement in Mexico, said before an exam, a game or a hard task. 'Echarle ganas' means to put real effort in.

dialog.es: Te va a ir muy bien.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend about to do something hard, like a race, a pitch or a first day.

spanish.pron: KOH-moh teh fweh en lah CHAM-bah

spanish.note: Literally 'I'm made into dust.' A common casual way to say you are exhausted. Women say 'hecha polvo.'
spanish.use: Say it after a short night or a long day, to a friend or coworker.

dare.title: Bike to the Bay for sunset
dare.why: Leave around 4:15 PM and take the Stevens Creek Trail to the water at Shoreline Park, so you're standing at the edge before the sun drops, a little after 5 PM. Watch the light turn the hills across the Bay orange. Phone stays in your pocket and no headphones until the last color is gone.
dare.worth: Open sky and water reset a day faster than almost anything, and the Bay's edge is close enough that most of us never actually go look. You'll remember an hour like this longer than most of today's tasks.

swap.title: Thank someone by hand
swap.why: Write three specific sentences on a real card or sticky note to someone who made your week easier, like a barista, a coworker or a neighbor, and hand it over today. Say exactly what they did.
swap.worth: A specific thank-you is rare enough to stick, and the person giving it usually enjoys it more than they expect.
